newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM's "study" groups received cash - report.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM's "study" groups received cash - report.

text.p: Two political fund-raising groups supporting Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto received cash totaling 4.5 million yen ($40,500) from groups indirectly linked to a company run by an executive at the centre of a health-care bribery scandal, a Japanese newspaper reported on Thursday.

The Mainichi Shimbun said during three years in the early 1990s, the two "study" groups received the money from two political groups in which Shiro Murata, former director and major shareholder of a company at the centre of a scandal, was involved.
Murata is a major shareholder and former director of Tokyo-based construction firm J.W.M, run by Hiroshi Koyama, who was arrested this month for allegedly bribing a senior health ministry official.
The two political groups donated a total of 76 million yen ($684,000) to a dozen politicians, including Hashimoto, the daily said.

The money included 10 million yen ($90,000) to a political faction led by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, 1.5 million yen ($13,500) to his fund-raising group, and 4.5 million yen ($40,500) to groups run by Health Minister Junichiro Koizumi, the daily said.
The newspaper report was published shortly after Hashimoto vowed to take bold steps towards bureaucratic reforms.

"In view of the situation that has disturbed the general public in the past several days, it's impossible to restore public trust in the administration without overhauling the entire system from the very bottom," Hashimoto told his party colleagues earlier on Thursday.
After his re-election this month, Hashimoto pledged to make bureaucratic reform one of the main pillars of his new government.
On Tuesday, a top bureaucrat resigned amid media reports that he took cash and other gifts from Koyama, who runs several private welfare institutions for ill elderly people.

Media reports said Nobuharu Okamitsu, the top bureaucrat in the powerful Health and Welfare Ministry, received 60 million yen ($540,000) in unreported donations, a golf club membership worth 13 million yen ($117,000) and the use of luxury cars from Koyama.
Since 1990, Koyama's old people's homes have been granted a total of 360 million yen ($3.24 million) in government subsidies for erecting specialised welfare institutions.
The media reports said Koyama boasted repeatedly about his ties to Health Ministry bureaucrats, who have the power over who is granted the subsidies. ($1=111 yen)
